data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is indefensible on Popper's own terms and constitutes a performative contradiction: acting on corroboration requires an inductive leap that past survival indicates future stability, smuggling induction back into the system whenever it leaves abstract methodology.","counterconditions":[{"case":"refuted if a coherent account can be provided where preferring a better-corroborated theory is justified solely as a method to maximize the severity of future tests without any assumption that the theory will actually succeed or remain unfalsified in the future","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if Popper explicitly distinguishes 'rational preference' based on critical scrutiny versus 'inductive inference' based on probability assignments","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if a definitive textual analysis shows Popper advised preference based on 'past performance' as a guide to 'future reliability' is a straw man","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By advising scientists to prefer the better-corroborated theory for action, Popper implicitly asserts that past performance is a reliable guide to future reliability.
